analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from restricting testimonials claiming foods or supplements cure or prevent disease, including in ads.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors, sent to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop any federal official from restricting the spread of testimonials in which a consumer says a food or dietary supplement mitigated, prevented, or cured something, based on that consumer's own experience. It overrides the main federal food and drug law and the FTC Act, and it explicitly covers testimonials a manufacturer puts in its own marketing. In practice it would let supplement and food companies use disease-cure and disease-prevention claims in ads as long as those claims are framed as someone's personal experience.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and marketers of dietary supplements and foods would gain the ability to use consumer testimonials claiming curative or preventive effects in their advertising, without federal agencies reviewing or restricting those claims.

how_it_helps.text: The bill says no federal official or employee may restrict dissemination of a testimonial containing a consumer's actual perception of the mitigative, preventive, or curative properties of any food or dietary supplement, overriding the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the Federal Trade Commission Act [S3].
It explicitly applies to dissemination by a manufacturer for purposes of marketing, not just to individual consumers speaking on their own [S3].
It adds a safe harbor: a person who reasonably believes their testimonial is covered cannot be found in violation of any federal law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, especially those shopping for treatments for serious conditions, would bear the cost: health claims dressed up as personal testimonials could not be challenged by the FDA or FTC, and unverified disease-cure messages could spread through advertising.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the FTC Act for these testimonials, removing the agencies' existing authority to restrict marketing that suggests a supplement can treat disease [S3].

Because it covers manufacturer marketing, companies could seed advertising with paid or selected customer stories presented as proof that a product cures or prevents disease, and the safe-harbor clause shields anyone who reasonably believes they are covered [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is framed as protecting personal free speech, but because it applies to manufacturer marketing, its main effect would be to loosen the rules that keep unverified disease claims out of supplement and food advertising. The cost falls on consumers trying to tell a tested treatment from a personal story in an ad; the benefit goes largely to marketers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat; it never came to the floor, and the Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Ron Paul introduced the bill in the House on September 13, 2011 [S5].

It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on September 13, 2011, and to that committee's Health Subcommittee on September 20, 2011; no further action was taken before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers are better off because the bill never passed: the FDA and FTC keep their existing authority over health claims in supplement and food marketing. Supplement marketers who wanted the advertising latitude did not get it.

for.name: Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; no other member cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, including its Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, then referred it to the Health Subcommittee, and never took it up for a markup or sent it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single sponsor and no cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would let them use testimonials claiming their products prevent, mitigate, or cure conditions in marketing, without FDA or FTC restriction. That gain comes at the public's cost of facing unverified disease claims in advertising.

Food companies could likewise use testimonial-based curative or preventive claims in advertising, since the bill defines 'food' by reference to the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. This would weaken the existing rules against such claims.

industries.industry: Advertising compliance and FTC/FDA enforcement of health claims
industries.note: The bill expressly overrides the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the FTC Act for these testimonials, removing a tool agencies use to police misleading health marketing.
